findings.evidence: Three child divs appear in this DOM order: #s3-step3 style="order:3" (text "Confirm your order"), #s3-step2 style="order:2" (text "Enter payment details"), #s3-step1 style="order:1" (text "Choose a plan")
findings.fix: Reorder the three .step divs in the markup so DOM order already reads Choose a plan, Enter payment details, Confirm your order, and drop the order declarations, or keep them only as a presentational refinement on top of markup that already reads correctly.
findings.violation: The step divs carry an inline order property that reverses the logical wizard sequence relative to DOM order: DOM order reads confirm, then pay, then choose a plan, exactly backwards from the real decision sequence (choose a plan, then pay, then confirm). A reader linearizing the DOM, such as a screen-reader user, hears the steps in the opposite order from the sequence the order values and the content itself imply, the same reversal WCAG-1.3.2 exists to catch.

findings.evidence: nav#nav contains exactly two links, "Plan a trip" (/plan) and "Service alerts" (/alerts); the page carries no search form, no sitemap link, no breadcrumb trail, and no related-links list anywhere else in the markup
findings.fix: Add a second independent way to locate this page or its content, such as a site search form or a breadcrumb trail that is not a duplicate of the primary navigation links.
findings.violation: The page exposes only one navigation mechanism, its primary nav menu, with no second independent mechanism such as a search form, sitemap, or breadcrumb trail, and nothing in the page's content marks it as one step of a linear process that would exempt it.

findings.evidence: Heading text "Schedule changes" introduces, among other content, #s3-wizard (a three-step "Choose a plan / Enter payment details / Confirm your order" sequence) and #s3-form (fields for route, email, phone, and a promo code)
findings.fix: Split the unrelated wizard and form content into their own appropriately-headed section, or reword the heading to cover everything the section actually contains.
findings.violation: The heading's wording describes schedule information, but the section it introduces also contains a purchase-style wizard (plan selection, payment, order confirmation) and a form collecting a promo code, none of which a reader scanning the heading could predict belongs here, and the mismatch persists across the whole section rather than one paragraph.

findings.evidence: input#promo aria-invalid="true" is paired with span#s3-form-promo-error aria-live="polite">Error.
findings.fix: Replace the error text with a specific description, for example "Promo code not recognized. Check for typos or re-enter the code from your offer."
findings.violation: The error text associated with the invalid promo field reads only "Error.", a generic message that identifies neither which rule the entered value failed nor what the reader should do differently, matching the criterion's own generic-text failure case.

findings.evidence: label for="phone" id="s3-form-phone-label" style="color:#cc0000">Phone number</label>, the only one of the form's four labels (Route, Email address, Phone number, Promo code) carrying any color styling
findings.fix: Add a visible non-color indicator next to the label, such as a required asterisk with accompanying text, or remove the color styling if it carries no meaning.
findings.violation: The phone label is distinguished from the form's other labels by color alone, with no accompanying text, icon, or symbol explaining what the red color signals, so a reader who cannot perceive that color gets no equivalent cue.

findings.evidence: Heading text "Accessibility improvements" is followed by #s1-p1 ("Riders may request a fare adjustment through the mobile app...") and #s1-p2 ("Passengers can check real time arrivals by calling rider services..."), neither of which describes an accessibility improvement
findings.fix: Reword the heading to match the section's actual content (for example "Fares and arrival information"), or move genuinely accessibility-related content into this section.
findings.violation: The heading's wording promises content about accessibility improvements, but the section's actual content is about fare adjustments and phone-based arrival checking, so a reader scanning headings cannot predict what the section actually covers.
